headline: Flight cancellations top 5,000 after FAA halt; Microsoft outage ends
briefing: U.S. airlines cancelled more than 5,000 flights on Saturday as they recovered from Friday's nationwide halt, and Air Canada says about 27,000 of its passengers were affected, so check any cross-border flight before heading to Pearson; schedules should be normal by the end of Sunday. Microsoft says the email outage that hit Toronto hospitals and offices since Thursday is fully over. Prime Minister Carney says a U.S. trade deal is closer but will not be signed without a viable auto sector, and Canada's October inflation report lands Monday.

keyDates.label: ASEAN summit opens; new municipal term
keyDates.why: The Southeast Asian summit Carney is attending opens in Manila, Ontario councils and the appointed regional chairs begin their four-year term, and the FAA expects U.S. flight schedules to be back to normal by the end of the day.

keyDates.label: Canada inflation report; OSAP bill expected
keyDates.why: Statistics Canada reports October consumer prices, the last reading before the Bank of Canada's next decision, and Ontario is expected to table its bill on student aid at private career colleges.

keyDates.label: APEC summit; Alaska ranked-choice count
keyDates.why: Leaders meet in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where Carney is to see Xi and the White House says Trump will meet Putin and Xi together; Alaska also tabulates its Peltola–Sullivan Senate race if no one tops 50%.

keyDates.label: Senate Democrats vote; Stelco recall
keyDates.why: Democratic senators choose between Chuck Schumer and Chris Van Hollen for majority leader by secret ballot, and 175 laid-off Stelco workers are due back in Hamilton.

keyDates.label: Bank of Canada and Fed rate decisions
keyDates.why: Both central banks decide the same day; high U.S. wholesale inflation and Monday's Canadian report will shape whether rates rise again.

keyDates.label: Lutnick testifies
keyDates.why: The U.S. commerce secretary is due before the Senate Banking Committee over delayed export restrictions in the Nvidia chip scandal.

stories.headline: More than 5,000 U.S. flights cancelled Saturday as FAA probes router failure
stories.summary: A day after the longest nationwide halt to U.S. departures since 2001, airlines cancelled more than 5,000 flights on Saturday and delayed over 14,000 as planes and crews remained out of place. Air Canada says it scrapped about 250 flights affecting roughly 27,000 passengers, and U.S. officials expect a full recovery by the end of Sunday.
stories.now: The tracking site FlightAware counted just over 5,000 U.S. cancellations and more than 14,600 delays by 1 p.m. Eastern on Saturday, at the top of the 4,000 to 5,000 range that Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) chief Bryan Bedford had forecast; about 160 Sunday flights had been cancelled by mid-afternoon. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a preliminary review points to a router that contractor L3Harris was installing at a remote FAA site while replacing copper lines with fibre, which flooded other routers and overloaded the network; investigators have not decided whether that was human error, a bad installation or faulty equipment, and officials again said there is no sign of a cyberattack. L3Harris said it is supporting the investigation and takes the disruption seriously. Duffy said such failures will recur unless Congress funds a US$50-billion overhaul of air traffic control, and the head of the controllers' union said communication with some aircraft was disrupted during the outage. In Canada, Air Canada said about 250 cancellations affected some 27,000 passengers and that a return to normal will take time; Toronto Pearson brought in extra staff, Porter offered refunds to customers who could not use rebooked flights, and airports in Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton and Halifax told travellers to check before leaving home.
stories.backstory: A ground stop is an order that keeps aircraft from taking off; planes already in the air continue to their destinations. Nationwide stops are very rare: CTV reported that Friday's was only the second halt of all U.S. departures since the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks, the other being a January 2023 failure of a pilot-notification system. The FAA's telecommunications network has caused regional stoppages before, including one in the Minneapolis area in August. Canada's own air traffic system was not affected, and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority said Pearson's systems were working normally. The outage came a day after an unrelated Microsoft email failure, and officials have not linked the two.

timeline.event: A notice-system outage causes the first nationwide U.S. ground stop since 2001
Telecommunications problem halts Minneapolis-area flights for about 90 minutes
FAA stops all U.S. departures at 3:54 p.m. Eastern; Pearson and Billy Bishop lose their cross-border flights
Order lifted at 8:15 p.m.; Duffy blames overloaded equipment and asks Congress for funding
Duffy blames a router installed during a contractor's fibre upgrade; cancellations top 5,000

stories.why: A single network fault stopped departures across the world's busiest aviation system for hours, which raises questions about the age and resilience of U.S. air traffic control equipment. The administration is using it to press Congress for modernization money, and officials have warned similar failures could recur without upgrades.
stories.impact: If you are flying between the GTA and the U.S. on Sunday or Monday, check your flight with the airline before leaving for Pearson or Billy Bishop, because aircraft and crews are still out of position and rebooked seats are scarce. Air Canada has warned that flights to the Caribbean and South America that cross U.S. airspace can also be affected. Under Canada's air passenger rules, airlines must rebook or refund you when a flight is cancelled, though cash compensation generally does not apply to disruptions outside the airline's control.

stories.headline: Carney: U.S. trade deal is closer, but not without a viable auto sector
stories.summary: Speaking in Manila on Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said talks with Washington are making progress and a two-country deal is possible, but that Canada is not there yet. He said he will not sign any agreement that fails to keep Canada's auto industry viable.
stories.now: Carney told reporters that keeping a viable Canadian auto sector is a condition Ottawa will not trade away, and described autos as one of the hardest issues in the negotiations. He said he recently had a substantive call with President Donald Trump that also included U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. CBC noted the comments come about three months after Canada walked away from talks when Washington made late demands that included concessions on autos. Carney also said his government is not satisfied with what he called the partial approach Stellantis has taken in Canada, a reference to the sale of the Brampton plant. No date for a deal or a next negotiating round was given, and Trump has threatened new tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles starting in January. Carney said a two-country deal with Washington is possible but that the sides are not there yet. Separately, Democrats who take control of Congress in January say repealing tariffs on Canadian goods is an early priority, with Rep. Jamie Raskin aiming for the first 100 days and Sen. Ron Wyden calling it a top goal, but they lack the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto and the plan targets only some of the tariff powers Trump has used.
stories.backstory: The United States has imposed tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, vehicles and other goods since 2025, and Canada answered with counter-tariffs plus relief programs for its own importers. Washington announced further tariffs on Canadian goods in July, and Canada pulled out of negotiations in the summer after last-minute U.S. demands. The North American trade pact known as CUSMA in Canada and USMCA in the United States is also under review. After Democrats won Congress on Nov. 3, Carney said the Trump administration is still the side Canada has to negotiate with.

timeline.event: U.S. announces new tariffs on Canadian goods

Stellantis announces sale of its Brampton plant; Ottawa widens tariff relief
Carney says the White House still leads on trade despite Democrats' win

stories.why: A deal with Washington would do more for the Canadian economy than any new agreement in Asia, because about three-quarters of Canada's exports go to the United States. Carney's condition signals that Ottawa would rather wait than accept terms that shrink auto assembly in Canada.
stories.impact: Ontario's auto plants and parts suppliers, including those in Brampton, Oakville, Oshawa, Alliston and Windsor, depend on tariff-free access to the U.S. market, so the terms on autos matter directly for jobs in the GTA. Until a deal is signed, existing tariffs and counter-tariffs stay in place, which keeps some vehicle, steel and consumer prices higher.

stories.headline: Carney says Ottawa is 'not satisfied' with Stellantis as rescue pitch for Brampton awaits CEO meeting
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday that his government is not satisfied with Stellantis's approach in Canada, and tied the future of the auto sector to trade talks with Washington. Ottawa and Ontario are still waiting to put their package to stop the Brampton plant sale to global chief executive Antonio Filosa.
stories.now: Speaking in Manila on Saturday, Carney said the government is in no way satisfied with the current situation or with what he called Stellantis's partial approach to its Canadian operations, and said Canada will not sign a U.S. trade deal that leaves the auto sector unviable. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Friday that Ottawa is still trying to find a way to prevent the sale to armoured-vehicle maker Roshel, working with Ontario and with Unifor, the union for more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada; she described the offer as an aggressive package but gave no details of what is in it. Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the aim of meeting Filosa is to buy some time by getting the company to slow the sale down, and that the province has not advanced any money for Brampton so far; he said any support for the scenarios Unifor has proposed would come from Ontario's existing $2.5-billion auto support fund. No date for the Filosa meeting has been announced. Joly has said Ottawa cannot block the sale under the Investment Canada Act because the seller is a Canadian subsidiary, so its leverage is the subsidy agreement: up to $529 million was committed in 2022 for the Brampton and Windsor plants, and Stellantis has offered to return $24 million. The 30-day default period began Thursday, and Stellantis expects the sale to close by the end of the year.
stories.backstory: The Brampton plant built Dodge and Chrysler cars and has been idle for about three years while workers stayed on paid layoff. In May 2022 Ottawa agreed to give Stellantis $529 million to retool its Brampton and Windsor plants, and the company had planned to build the Jeep Compass in Brampton. In October 2025 it moved that vehicle to Illinois as U.S. tariffs on Canadian-made cars took hold. Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel in September, Unifor's contract expired Sept. 20, and the union declared an impasse over the plant's future.

timeline.event: Stellantis signs memorandum with Roshel; Unifor contract expires

Carney says Ottawa is not satisfied with Stellantis's approach in Canada

stories.why: The sale ends hopes that a major GTA auto plant would restart vehicle production, and it tests whether governments can enforce the conditions attached to public subsidies. It also shows how U.S. tariffs are pulling auto investment out of Ontario.
stories.impact: Thousands of Peel Region families depend on the plant and its parts suppliers, and most laid-off workers have no guarantee of a job with the new owner. Taxpayers have a stake on both sides: any new support package would be public money, and the gap between the $24 million Stellantis has offered and what Ottawa says it is owed may end up in court.

stories.headline: Microsoft says email and Teams fully restored after outage that hit Toronto hospitals
stories.summary: Microsoft said early Saturday that Outlook, Teams and its other online services are fully back after a worldwide outage that began Thursday and lasted more than 24 hours for some users. The company apologized and blamed a fault during a network upgrade, not a cyberattack.
stories.now: Microsoft said it had finished fixing the underlying problem and restored service to the last affected customers and regions; reports based on the Associated Press put full restoration at 1:09 a.m. Eastern on Saturday. The company said it was deeply sorry and traced the failure to a problem that arose during a network capacity upgrade after a recent network change, adding that neither a cyberattack nor artificial-intelligence agents were involved. It has promised a full report once its review is done. The outage, which also knocked out the Copilot assistant, drew more than 20,000 problem reports in Canada and affected federal departments, VIA Rail and Toronto's Unity Health hospitals, which declared a Code Grey on Thursday; abroad it disrupted government agencies in the United States, Japan, Australia and Singapore, slowed trading firms and prompted airlines to warn of communication delays.
stories.backstory: Many hospitals, universities, governments and businesses rent email and office software from Microsoft as an online service, known as Microsoft 365, rather than running their own servers. That means a single fault at the company can hit thousands of organizations at once. In July 2024 a faulty update from security firm CrowdStrike crashed Windows computers worldwide and disrupted GTA hospitals and airports. Ontario hospitals use Code Grey to signal the loss of essential infrastructure such as power, water or computer systems.

timeline.event: CrowdStrike update crashes Windows systems worldwide, hitting GTA hospitals
Outlook outage begins; Unity Health Toronto declares Code Grey
Microsoft says recovery is not working as expected
Unity Health says email is restored; Microsoft warns of lingering delays
Microsoft declares all services restored and apologizes

stories.why: The outage shows how much hospitals, schools and governments depend on one company's online services for basic communication. A long disruption slows everything from appointment notices to internal approvals.
stories.impact: If your workplace, school or hospital uses Outlook, messages sent between Thursday and early Saturday may have arrived late or out of order, so re-check anything time-sensitive and phone to confirm appointments. Hospital care in Toronto continued throughout, and Microsoft says there is no sign of an attack or of lost data.

stories.headline: Iran now reports four tankers hit by mines; Trump said to be holding off on new strikes
stories.summary: Iranian forces say at least four oil tankers, one of them a supertanker, have exploded or caught fire after striking mines in and near the Strait of Hormuz; none of the claims has been independently confirmed. Reuters-sourced reports say President Trump has told advisers he may hold off on attacking Iran unless there are new provocations.
stories.now: Counts differ: Iran's military spoke of fires on three tankers, while later reports citing the Revolutionary Guards put the number at four or more, including a supertanker in the southern part of the strait. No ship has been named, Reuters said it could not verify the reports, and the U.S. military says it has cleared the main shipping lanes. British maritime monitors say traffic through the strait is still about 65% below pre-war levels. Three people familiar with the matter said Trump has told senior advisers in recent days that he may refrain from new attacks if Iran and Yemen's Houthis do not provoke one, and that Gulf states have urged restraint; a White House official said only Trump knows what he will do. Separately, U.S. Central Command said it shot down two Iranian attack drones headed for Bahrain on Friday and denied Iran's claim to have hit two radar sites there. Brent crude ended Friday near US$96 a barrel; markets reopen Monday, and Trump plans to raise the war with Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen next week.
stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran choked traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened it but collapsed in July, and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25. Trump has said the war will end soon, one way or the other.

timeline.event: Qatar hands Iran a new draft deal

stories.why: Oil prices are the main driver of higher inflation in Canada and the U.S.; the October spike is why the Bank of Canada raised rates on Oct. 28.
stories.impact: Lower crude usually reaches GTA gas pumps within days, and this month's drop has eased fuel and delivery costs. With talks stalled and tankers reportedly hitting mines, that relief could reverse when markets reopen Monday, though signs that Trump may hold off on new strikes work the other way.

stories.headline: Peltola's Alaska lead tops 10,000 votes; Democrats will hold 30 governorships
stories.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola widened her lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the last uncalled U.S. Senate race, but remains just under the 50% needed to win outright. The Associated Press has called Alaska's governorship for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.
stories.now: The latest Associated Press count gives Peltola 138,240 votes, or 49.84%, to Sullivan's 127,828, or 46.09%, with about 96% of ballots counted; her lead grew to 10,412 votes from about 5,800 a day earlier. The AP has not called the race, and if no one passes 50% a ranked-choice tabulation on Nov. 18 will redistribute the votes of trailing candidates. A Peltola win would give Democrats 56 of 100 Senate seats. The AP called the governor's race Friday evening for Kreiss-Tomkins, a 37-year-old former state legislator who had 50.8% to 28.1% for Trump-endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson; he replaces term-limited Republican Mike Dunleavy on Dec. 7 and brings the number of Democratic governors to 30. Alaska plans to certify results on Nov. 25. Earlier in the week Democrats also won the Kansas governorship and Mississippi's Senate seat, and they take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers since January 2025, and all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate were on the ballot. More than 53 million Americans voted early. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war weighed on Trump's approval, and recent polls gave Democrats an edge in most key Senate races. Courts also turned back a Trump administration bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots.

timeline.event: Supreme Court rejects bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots

stories.why: An Alaska win would add to the Senate majority Democrats take over in January, on top of Colom's victory in a state Republicans had held for more than four decades. A bigger majority makes it easier for them to block nominees, run investigations and force votes on tariffs.
stories.impact: Canadian exporters are watching whether a Democratic Congress moves to limit tariffs, which could ease pressure on Ontario manufacturers over time; near-term tariffs stay in place unless the White House changes them.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says U.S. raised trading Donbas for NATO membership; Europe names its negotiating team
stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that U.S. negotiators asked whether Ukraine would give up the eastern Donbas region in exchange for joining NATO, the first time the two issues have been linked in the talks. European Union leaders agreed that Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, with EU officials, will represent Europe in future negotiations.
stories.now: Zelenskyy said the question came up during this week's U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi and repeated that Kyiv is not prepared to give up territory. He said he would put such a question to a national referendum only as part of a full package that included security guarantees, a strong and well-funded army and money for reconstruction. Russia has long opposed NATO membership for Ukraine and cited it as a reason for its 2022 invasion. Zelenskyy said the areas of the Donbas the Americans asked about are ones Russia does not currently control, and that it was the first time NATO membership had been tied to giving up land in these talks. At their summit in Ireland, EU leaders settled on a team of five military powers (Britain, which is outside the EU, plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland) and EU officials to speak for Europe, resolving a question left open on Friday; Zelenskyy welcomed it, while the Kremlin has not fully accepted a European role. The Abu Dhabi round ended Wednesday without agreement on territory but with a prisoner exchange covering more than 1,000 people, and there was no word of progress on a halt to strikes on energy sites after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
stories.backstory: U.S.-mediated efforts to end the war stalled for months while Washington focused on Iran. Rubio said in May that the effort had stagnated. Europe has repeatedly asked to be included in any deal affecting its own security.

timeline.event: Rubio says peace effort has stagnated

stories.why: Linking NATO membership to land is a new idea in the talks and touches the two issues that have blocked a settlement: territory and Ukraine's long-term security. Any change to NATO's membership would need the agreement of all allies, including Canada.
stories.impact: Peace progress could ease energy and grain prices over time. Canada, a NATO and G7 member, would have a vote on any Ukrainian membership and would share in the security commitments that came with it.

stories.headline: Republican pressure on Lutnick grows over Nvidia chip scandal; Trump still backs him
stories.summary: Axios reported Saturday that the sharpest criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over delayed export curbs on an Nvidia customer is now coming from Republicans in Congress, fellow cabinet members and President Trump's own base. There is no sign that Trump has withdrawn his support.
stories.now: Axios reported that Trump supported acting against Megaspeed International on three occasions and that Lutnick's department delayed each effort; the Commerce Department has called accounts of the dispute inaccurate. Bessent told CNBC that Treasury, the State and Defense departments and the U.S. Trade Representative had for months favoured adding Megaspeed International to an export-control list, but that Commerce is in charge of that decision. CNN reported Friday that Trump advisers have discussed whether Lutnick should go and that the president has taken calls from officials and outside allies raising concerns; CNBC reported that Trump is standing by him for now. CNBC also reported that Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick used to lead and that his sons now run, has business ties to Nvidia, which an ethics expert said raises questions. Reuters has reported that Megaspeed bought more than US$4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced chips since June 2024; the company denies wrongdoing, and the Commerce Department denies an Axios account of a Situation Room confrontation between the two secretaries. Republican Sen. John Kennedy wants to know why the sales were approved, and Huang has agreed to testify to a House committee in a closed session by U.S. Thanksgiving (Nov. 26). Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10. Chief financial officer Colette Kress remains interim chief executive while the board searches for a successor.
stories.backstory: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has run it since 1993, building it into the main supplier of the chips used to train artificial intelligence (AI) systems and one of the world's most valuable companies. Earlier this week, reports said the company had opened an internal investigation into whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort through a relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told staff in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The stock had already slipped on that first report before Wednesday's news.

timeline.event: Board opens independent probe after report Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence

stories.why: Nvidia is central to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom and one of the largest stocks in major U.S. indexes, and it has never had another chief executive. The spying allegation also raises national-security questions in Washington, which controls what chips the company may sell to China.
stories.impact: Most Canadian pension plans, index funds and RRSP or TFSA portfolios that track U.S. stocks hold Nvidia, so its swings show up in retirement savings here. The company's next results and its CEO search could bring more volatility.

stories.headline: Three children and two adults critically hurt in Burlington townhouse fire
stories.summary: Five people, including three children, are in life-threatening condition after a fire in a Burlington townhouse early Saturday. Ontario's Fire Marshal is investigating and no cause has been given.
stories.now: Halton police said the fire broke out shortly before 7 a.m. at a townhouse complex at 1300 Maple Crossing Blvd., near Freeman Street. Burlington firefighters pulled the occupants out and put the fire out before it spread to neighbouring units. Two adults and three children were taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries; CBC reported that three of the patients had no vital signs when first reached and are now listed as critical, and paramedics said a sixth person had lesser injuries. Police have not confirmed the children's ages. Fire Chief Drew Boys said the investigation is at an early stage and that nothing has been ruled out, including whether the fire was suspicious and whether smoke alarms were working.
stories.backstory: The fire was in a multi-unit townhouse complex in central Burlington, a city of about 190,000 people in Halton Region west of Toronto. In Ontario, the Office of the Fire Marshal investigates fires that cause deaths or serious injuries, working alongside local police and fire services. Those investigations look at where a fire started, what caused it and whether smoke alarms were installed and working. Ontario law requires a working smoke alarm on every storey of a home and outside all sleeping areas.

timeline.event: Fire reported at Maple Crossing Blvd. townhouse shortly before 7 a.m.
Firefighters rescue occupants; five taken to hospital in life-threatening condition
Ontario Fire Marshal called in; cause not yet known

stories.why: Five people from one home, three of them children, are fighting for their lives, and investigators have not yet said how the fire started. The findings on cause and on smoke alarms could matter for fire-safety enforcement in similar housing.
stories.impact: There is no continuing danger to neighbours, but expect police and fire crews around Maple Crossing Boulevard while the investigation continues. It is a reminder to test smoke alarms on every floor and to make sure everyone at home knows two ways out.

stories.headline: Canada's October inflation report lands Monday, with forecasts from 3.0% to 3.3%
stories.summary: Statistics Canada reports October consumer prices on Monday, the last inflation reading before the Bank of Canada's Dec. 9 rate decision. Economists expect the annual rate to stay close to September's 3.1%, but disagree on whether high energy costs are spreading to other prices.
stories.now: A Reuters poll of economists points to 3.2%, up from 3.1% in September. RBC expects a slight easing to 3.0%, with core inflation, which strips out volatile items, slipping to 1.9% from 2.1%; Continuum Economics forecasts 3.3%, which would be the highest since December 2023. Desjardins economist LJ Valencia expects a reading similar to or slightly above September's. CIBC's Avery Shenfeld and Helen Lao argue inflation will not climb as much as the Bank of Canada projects, which would leave less need for more rate increases. The central bank has said it expects inflation to stay above 3% through much of 2027, and one market report Friday put the odds of a December hike at about 64%.
stories.backstory: Oil prices jumped after the U.S.-Iran war disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz this year, and fuel costs have pushed up inflation since. Canada's annual rate rose to 3.1% in September, led by gasoline, while core measures stayed near 2%. On Oct. 28 the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years, and said more hikes were possible. Oil has since fallen from a late-October peak above US$117 to the mid-US$90s.

timeline.event: Inflation at 3.0%
September inflation reported at 3.1%
Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%
October inflation report due
Next Bank of Canada rate decision

stories.why: Monday's number is the main piece of evidence the Bank of Canada will have before deciding whether to raise rates again. A reading above 3.2% with firmer core prices would strengthen the case for a hike.
stories.impact: If you have a variable-rate mortgage or line of credit, or are renewing soon, this report will shape what happens to your payments in December. It will also show whether October's fuel spike reached grocery and other prices in Ontario.

stories.headline: Canada and the Philippines finish free-trade talks; signing targeted for 2027
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced in Manila on Saturday that negotiations on a Canada-Philippines free trade agreement are complete, with both sides aiming to sign it next year. Ottawa also says talks on a wider deal with the Southeast Asian bloc are substantially concluded, though that agreement is not yet final.
stories.now: The two countries' trade ministers signed a joint statement closing the negotiations while Carney and Marcos looked on, about a year after the talks were restarted. Carney said the deal could help triple two-way trade to more than $10 billion a year by 2035, from about $2.4 billion in 2025, and that both governments will move quickly to sign it and bring it into force in 2027. The text has not been released, and the Globe and Mail reported there was no word on whether Canada will be exempted from temporary limits on pork imports that Manila is bringing in this month; Canada sold about $279 million of pork products to the Philippines in 2024. On the broader agreement with the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Prime Minister's Office says negotiations are substantially concluded and a Philippine official said they had wrapped up, while other reports note it has not been finalized. The ASEAN summit opens Sunday; Carney then goes to the Francophonie summit in Phnom Penh and to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on Nov. 18–19, where he is to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.
stories.backstory: Canada and the Philippines first discussed a trade agreement in 2015, and Carney and Marcos agreed in October 2025 to restart and speed up the talks, alongside a separate Canada-ASEAN negotiation. The push is part of Ottawa's effort to find customers beyond the United States as tariffs from the Trump administration hit Canadian exports. The Asia trip also takes Carney to China, where he has said he will raise foreign interference with Xi; a federal public inquiry found China was the most active foreign state trying to interfere in Canadian democratic institutions. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has criticized the travel, saying the economy is about people struggling to make ends meet rather than summits.

timeline.event: Carney and Marcos agree to restart and speed up trade talks
The two leaders pledge in Vancouver to finish negotiations by year-end
Carney meets European leaders in Dublin, then leaves for Asia
Canada and the Philippines announce negotiations are concluded; Ottawa says ASEAN talks substantially concluded
APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen, where Carney is to meet Xi
Target for signing the Canada-Philippines agreement

stories.why: It is the first concrete result of a trip meant to show Canada can rely less on the United States for trade. Concluding talks is not the same as a deal in force: the agreement still has to be signed and ratified, and its tariff schedule has not been published.
stories.impact: Nothing changes at the border yet, so prices and tariffs stay as they are until the agreement is signed and ratified, likely not before 2027. The Philippines is one of the largest sources of new immigrants to the GTA, so lower barriers could eventually matter for local importers, food businesses and Ontario exporters, including pork producers.

stories.headline: Two former environment ministers dispute Dabrusin's claim that Canada is on course for Paris
stories.summary: Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said at the United Nations climate talks in Turkey that Canada remains committed to its Paris Agreement pledges. Her Liberal predecessors Catherine McKenna and Steven Guilbeault publicly rejected that description.
stories.now: Dabrusin made the comment to The Canadian Press from the COP31 climate conference in Antalya. McKenna called the statement factually untrue, and Guilbeault said it defies reason, pointing to modelling by the Canadian Climate Institute; reports cited by the critics indicate Canada is unlikely to hit its 2030 target. Dabrusin's office replied that the government stands by the Paris Agreement and is committed to reaching net-zero emissions by 2050, without directly addressing the 2030 goal. Prime Minister Mark Carney said in June that the previous government's climate policies had been too costly and divisive.
stories.backstory: Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries set their own targets for cutting the greenhouse gases that warm the planet. Canada has promised to cut emissions 40% to 45% below 2005 levels by 2030 and to reach net zero, meaning no more emissions than are removed, by 2050. Since taking office Carney has dropped or loosened several Trudeau-era measures, including the consumer carbon price, while backing new energy projects. McKenna was environment minister from 2015 to 2019, and Guilbeault held the job from 2021 to 2025 before leaving cabinet last year over a pipeline agreement with Alberta.

timeline.event: Canada signs the Paris Agreement
Ottawa raises its 2030 target to a 40–45% cut from 2005 levels
Guilbeault quits cabinet over pipeline deal with Alberta
Carney calls earlier climate policies too costly and divisive
McKenna and Guilbeault reject Dabrusin's statement from COP31

stories.why: It is unusual for two former ministers from the governing party to publicly contradict a sitting minister on a core commitment. The dispute puts pressure on Ottawa to say plainly whether the 2030 target still stands.
stories.impact: Nothing changes immediately for Ontario households. Over time, how seriously Ottawa pursues the 2030 target affects fuel and heating rules, rebates for electric vehicles and heat pumps, and the regulations facing Ontario industry.

sources.title: Global News: Former environment minister says Canada's commitment to climate targets 'factually untrue'

stories.headline: U.S. wholesale inflation hits 6.5%; stocks slip Friday but end the week higher
stories.summary: Prices charged by U.S. producers rose 0.3% in October and 6.5% from a year earlier, the biggest annual increase since November 2022. The S&P 500 fell 0.4% and the Nasdaq 0.9% on Friday, though all three main U.S. indexes still gained more than 2% on the week.
stories.now: The U.S. producer price index, which tracks what businesses receive for goods and services before they reach shoppers, rose 0.3% in October, a little under the 0.4% economists expected; the 6.5% annual rate compared with a 6.6% forecast. Leaving out food and energy, prices were up 0.3% on the month and 5% on the year, and wholesale food prices jumped 1.3%, the most since February. At Friday's close the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.1% at about 52,347, the S&P 500 down 0.4% at 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq down 0.9% at 25,136.27, with chipmakers leading the declines, according to Yahoo Finance and the Associated Press; for the week the S&P 500 gained about 2.5%, the Nasdaq 2.3% and the Dow 2.1%. In Toronto, the S&P/TSX Composite Index slipped 0.09% to 36,105.90 and was up about 0.9% on the week. U.S. coverage says the data keeps the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates in December, and one market report put the odds of a Bank of Canada increase that month at about 64%.
stories.backstory: Wholesale prices often signal where consumer prices are heading a few months later. Oil surged after the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, with Brent crude peaking above US$117 in late October, and tariffs have added to import costs. The Federal Reserve held its rate on Oct. 28, the same day the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5%, its first increase in more than three years. Canada's annual inflation rate was 3.1% in September.

timeline.event: Iran war begins; oil prices start climbing
Canada's inflation rate edges up to 3.1%
Fed holds; Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%
U.S. 10-year Treasury yield rises to about 5.09%
U.S. wholesale inflation reported at 6.5% for October
S&P 500 closes down 0.4%, Nasdaq down 0.9%; TSX ends at 36,105.90

stories.why: Persistent price pressure in the United States makes further interest-rate increases there more likely. Canadian bond yields and mortgage rates tend to follow U.S. ones, and the Bank of Canada decides on the same day as the Fed, Dec. 9.
stories.impact: If you are renewing a mortgage or carrying a variable-rate loan in Ontario, higher U.S. rates raise the odds of higher borrowing costs here. Rising U.S. wholesale food prices can also feed into grocery bills, since Ontario imports much of its fresh produce from the U.S.

stories.headline: Merkley joins Van Hollen's backers; Schumer still leads public endorsements 14 to 5
stories.summary: Oregon Sen. Jeff Merkley became the latest Democrat to back Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen's challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader. Public counts still show Schumer well ahead before the Dec. 1 secret ballot.
stories.now: Merkley endorsed Van Hollen on Friday afternoon, joining Sen. Bernie Sanders, Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan. Axios counts 14 senators publicly behind Schumer, including himself, against five for Van Hollen; Nevada Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto has backed Schumer and Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego has said he will. Mississippi Sen.-elect Scott Colom has not committed to Schumer, and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin has declined to back him without endorsing Van Hollen. Two unions that together represent about 700,000 members have endorsed Van Hollen, who says more than 10 senators have privately pledged support. Schumer, 75, says he has the votes to stay on, and prediction markets on Friday put his chances at roughly 83% to 87%. Other outlets' tallies differ slightly, with the Washington Examiner counting 15 for Schumer and four for Van Hollen; the winner will need 28 or 29 votes depending on the Alaska result, and the ballot is secret.
stories.backstory: Schumer, of New York, has led Senate Democrats since 2017, as majority leader from 2021 to 2025 and minority leader since. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterms and take over in January. Schumer faced criticism within his party during the campaign, and Van Hollen broke with party leadership by endorsing El-Sayed in Michigan's Democratic primary in June. Whoever leads the majority decides which bills and nominees reach the Senate floor.

timeline.event: Van Hollen backs El-Sayed in Michigan, breaking with party leaders
Democrats win control of the Senate and House
Van Hollen announces challenge; Schumer says he has the votes
Sanders and Merkley endorse Van Hollen; public counts still favour Schumer
Senate Democrats scheduled to vote by secret ballot

stories.why: The majority leader controls the Senate's agenda, including whether and when votes on tariffs, spending and oversight of the White House happen. The contest is the first test of unity for Democrats since their midterm win.
stories.impact: There is no direct effect on Ontario for now. The winner will shape how hard the Senate pushes back on tariffs against Canada when the new Congress sits in January.
